newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish financial markets focus on 1998 budget gap.
newsitem.headline: Polish financial markets focus on 1998 budget gap.

text.p: The uncertain level of next year's Polish budget deficit will occupy the country's financial markets in coming weeks with the central bank seen slowly tightening the monetary screws.

Analysts said on Friday that the level of next year's budget deficit could ultimately determine just how restrictive the central bank's monetary policy must be in order to steer Poland away from a Czech-style current account crisis.
"Next year's budget could be the key because a bigger deficit translates into higher central bank rates and yields," said Wojciech Kowalczyk, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Strongly-worded statements by the central bank, backed by the OECD and the IMF, have called on the government to slash next year's budget gap to 1.5 percent of GDP and to balance its books by 1999 to curb Poland's booming domestic demand.

But the government, in the heat of a tough election campaign, has said its plan of 1.9 percent of GDP deficit in 1998, against a 1997 gap forecast of 2.8 percent, would sufficiently cool internal demand and imports with it.
After parliamentary polls on September 21, the 1998 budget plan will be examined by a post-election government, which will likely have little time to make sweeping changes in the draft.

This week the National Bank of Poland (NBP) incrased market rates by about half a percentage point to about 23 percent, trying to offset a large cash injection into the economy from the government's flood recovery programme.
"Reverse repo rates and NBP-bill yields should remain around 23 percent for the time being after this week's rise," said Aleksandra Watroba, dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
Dealers said the central bank might further push market rates higher, or up obligatory reserves on banks, only after evaluating the effects of this week's increases.

"If the central bank increased market rates to quickly, they may hit the 25 percent Lombard rate, and force the NBP to increase nominal rates, which it doesn't want to do," said one analyst in Warsaw.

Analysts said an increase in nominal rates, now at 22 and 25 percent, might not be effective because it would bring in large amounts of speculative foreign capital and encourage the private sector to borrow in foreign currencies.
The zloty was expected to trade in a range between the parity rate and its support, set by Thursday's central bank intervention at minus 1.5 percent from parity.
"The zloty may stabilise in a narrower range around minus1.0 percent next week after two weeks of turbulence," said Piotr Czyzewski, dealer at ING Bank in Warsaw.

Some said the zloty would continue to be moved mainly by currency speculators, who cashed in on the local currency's nearly five percent rise over the last 10 days following sharp falls during the initial stages of the flood crisis.
"Longer-term investors are not interested in Poland before the elections and any foreign entry is likely to be more speculative in nature," Handlowy's Kowalczyk said.
On Friday the zloty closed at minus 0.8 percent from the parity rate, stronger than last week's close at minus 2.9 percent.

Dealers expected yields to continue to rise at Monday's 1.1 billion zloty primary T-bill tender amid little interest from foreign and domestic investors, who can purchase comparable treasuries at higher rates on the secondary market.

The 52-week T-bill yield was seen around 22.25 percent from last week's 22.09 and the 13-week T-bill could rise to 21.90 percent from 21.70 on the back of this week's rise in the 91-day NBP-bill to 23.00 percent.
